Found it 'a little bit fishy' that you can only tell skills.sh is from Vercel by clicking the top-left corner, and that the top two skills are Vercel's despite more widely used skills existing elsewhere. Said the UI looks nice, though.
Criticized the ranking: skills are ordered by install counts from Vercel's own tool rather than by quality. 'Famously good signal for quality... Not even npm, their own tools download count.'
The leaderboard is ranked by weekly downloads through the 'npx skills' command, which is Vercel's new 'standard' installer, so their own skills are obviously at the top.
After the ranking method was explained, the user said that explanation 'would have been nice' to have on the site and that the leaderboard is misleading without it.
As someone who finds skills useful, they said listings like the codex skill on skills.sh raise the same question MCP did: why not just have the agent run 'tool --help'?

Called it nice work but noted Vercel isn't first. Suggested that hovering a row should show the skill description plus a copy-install-command button. Compared it to claudemarketplaces.com (shows descriptions and copy-to-install in the list) and skillsmp.com (77K+ skills, but search is hidden behind cryptic buttons).
'Great work on this btw, the agent-agnostic approach is the right call.'
Alternative approach: 'I've been using Nix to manage my skills instead. It's been great,' especially because it declaratively manages the CLI tools and MCPs that skills depend on.
Feature request for skills.sh: 'Please make a rest API!'

Complained that these 'npm for Skills' tools don't document basic package management such as updates, version pinning, or uninstalls: 'If I use this skills.sh tool to install the Foo Skill for one or more agent harness, how do I update Foo later?'
Said the best workaround they've found for multi-agent installation is symlinks, and that 'this tool doesn't seem to even try to solve the updating or versioning requirements.'
'This is a really good implementation,' but they don't rely heavily on other people's skills. They questioned instructions like 'pick an extreme' in the design skill featured on the homepage.
Replying to the discussion of updating and versioning: 'Skills certainly got a wildwest pre VCS copy-paste feeling going on.'
